title: Jalen Brunson Shares How He is a ‘Star Role Player’ After Accepting Limited Responsibilities With Mavs
description: There are a number of success stories in the NBA, and Jalen Brunson is arguably one of the most relatable. fullText:
There are a number of success stories in the NBA, and Jalen Brunson is arguably one of the most relatable.

The New York Knicks star led the team to a championship after a 23-year drought. While all five members of the starting lineup played like there was no tomorrow, stepping up as heroes in each of their four wins in the final dance, Brunson played the biggest role.

He was the smallest player on the court, something critic think is his ultimate disadvantage. Still his heart was big enough to make 7-foot-4 Victor Wembanyama tremble. It was a scenario that seemed impossible for him just four years ago.

Brunson came to the league in 2018 after a successful college career with the Villanova Wildcats. The Dallas Mavericks drafted him 33rd overall, and there weren't many expectations surrounding him, especially because the Mavs selected future superstar Luka Doncic in the same draft.

He accepted that role, but how he embraced it is what made the difference.

In an interview with the Road Trippin' show, the 2026 Finals MVP shared that he saw himself in another undersized guard, J.J. Barea, when he was handed a reserve point guard role.

"My mindset was, I'm filling JJ Barea's role. He came off the bench for Dallas. He did all these great things for Dallas.," he said.

"That's where I see myself. I'm gonna work to be better, but that's where I see myself. That's where I feel like I can help this team."

He excelled in that role. By his fourth year in Dallas, he had nearly doubled his production, going from 9.3 points per game during his rookie season to 16.3 in 2022.

Brunson believes his dedication to fulfilling the responsibilities of a role player gave him more opportunities to showcase his talent.

"The more you show in your role, the longer your leash gets, the more you're able to do. People just want to say, 'Hey, I can do this, I can do that.' Well, do what's asked of you first. Perfect it. Master it," he said.

"And all of a sudden you'll be surprised of what they'll allow you to do. And you'll be surprised by yourself, like, 'oh damn, I can do this.'"

After that, he signed with the Knicks. He is now a bona fide star.

He averaged 24 points per game in his first season in the Big Apple and 28.7 points per game the following season. He has been an All-Star in each of the last three seasons.

He is no longer a role player. Now, it is the role players who base their roles around him.

title: ‘Energy Level is High’ – 76ers Core Hold Workout Together and Jaylen Brown Can’t Contain His Excitement About His Group
description: Philadelphia 76ers fans have every reason to be excited about the upcoming season. They landed LeBron James and Jaylen Brown this summer. fullText:
Philadelphia 76ers fans have every reason to be excited about the upcoming season. They landed LeBron James and Jaylen Brown this summer.

Chemistry is their next challenge, but it looks like it will not be much of a problem.

NBA training camp will officially begin on September 29, but several teams have already taken steps to build chemistry through workouts on their own time. The Sixers' core players are among them.

Brown said he has been working out with his new teammates, and he has a simple way of letting their supporters know that they are going to be good.

"We've been working, building chemistry with the guys. Maxey is a dog. LeBron is the goat, you don't even need to say what LeBron is. He look good, healthy," he said.

"This was one of our first workouts, but we worked out a few times. You can feel the energy level is high, the talent is high."

Brown and James join a team that surprised last season. The Sixers ended the regular season as the No. 2 seed and survived the play-in tournament to face JB's former team, the Boston Celtics. They went down 1-3 but still managed to beat them in seven games, powered by Joel Embiid's huge playoff performances and All-Star Tyrese Maxey.

Brown has been outspoken about the upcoming season following his shocking trade to the Sixers. He has released most of his statements through his Twitch streaming account.

In his latest episode, he expressed how mentally ready he is to play for the Sixers and how willing he is to make sacrifices to help them win a championship.

"Whatever the team needs, I'll be listening and waiting, but my mentality is to kill, you know what I mean? I feel like I want blood this year. I feel like that's the mentality: I want blood," he said.

Brown, James, Embiid, and Maxey are all expected to be part of the Sixers' starting five. They will be joined by VJ Edgecombe.

As for the bench, general manager Mike Gansey has added Anfernee Simons, Caleb Love, and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope. The team also has Dean Wade, Jabari Walker, and Justin Edwards.

ESPN's championship odds have the 76ers as the best team in the Eastern Conference, tied with the defending champion New York Knicks.

title: West Ham 4-2 Wolves - fans' verdict
description: We asked for your thoughts after Tuesday's Championship match between West Ham United and Wolverhampton Wanderers.
fullText:
We asked for your thoughts after Tuesday's Championship match between West Ham United and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Here are some of your comments:

Woody: The game was a lottery as both defences were poor, but we managed to score more. We need to massively improve in defence if we're going to get promoted.

Dave: At last a better team effort, moving the ball quicker, but the new players we need didn't arrive.

At times the back four were wanting and the real big problem is that we don't have enough cover - what happened to finding full-back cover?

All we can do now is hope this team can continue with winning, but I am really concerned.

Sue: Much-improved display. The players need to gel and then will be a good competitive team. Still starting slow. That needs addressing.

Tristan: Didn't offer much at the back and were not clinical going forward at all. Played our hardest game of the season at a good time, and didn't make the most of it.

Steve: Overall I don't think we were that bad, certainly not 4-2 bad. We lost to yet another worldie, a daft, unnecessary penalty and a deflection, plus we hit the bar twice. It's a long season and it's going to be a rollercoaster - buckle up and stay positive.

Peter: Wolves will not be in the promotion stakes unless they tighten up their defence, which was cruelly exposed by the Hammers after looking suspect in the opening games. The retention of a focused Krejci and his return to the starting line-up could certainly help in that respect.

title: New York Giants' Darius Slayton addresses ongoing trade rumors
description: New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton shrugs off ongoing trade rumors and talks Odell Beckham Jr.
fullText:
Wide receiver Darius Slayton, the New York Giants' longest-tenured player, isn't about to let the recent trade rumors bother him. He's been the subject of that kind of talk before and has gotten used to it.

"It's not the first time, probably won't be the last time. But I really don't pay it too much of mind, honestly. I just take it day by day," he told reporters on Tuesday.

Slayton, 29, is entering the middle season of a three-year, $36 million deal with a $15.9 million salary cap hit for 2026. Those figures worked against the Giants in any trade talks. But they are working in Slayton's favor now. The Giants were rumored to be willing to move the former 2019 fifth-round pick out of Auburn this summer, but, as stated, his salary likely deterred any suitors.

The Giants had a glut of wideouts in camp and, even though Slayton was returning from sports hernia surgery this offseason, he was going to be included in the team's plans unless he could be moved in a trade. He made the Giants' 53-man roster this past weekend.

"I thought he played well. Had a heck of a camp," head coach John Harbaugh said. "He's a great guy, great player, hard worker, and did a heck of a job like he's always done here."

Slayton is just one of five wide receivers the Giants are carrying on their active roster, along with Malik Nabers, Malachi Fields, Darnell Mooney, and Odell Beckham Jr.

The 33-year-old Beckham's presence means Slayton is no longer the elder statesman in the Giants' wide receiver room.

Slayton came to the Giants the season after Beckham left via a trade with Cleveland. He is looking forward to playing with the former Pro Bowler and fan favorite.

"I think it's a beautiful thing for him to come back here,' said Slayton. "Obviously, the fans love him. If you're a football fan, you probably love him because he was such an iconic player. It's definitely awesome to see him get his chance to come back."

title: Woltemade move underlines summer of change at Newcastle
description: It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day as Nick Woltemade left Newcastle United to join Juventus on loan and the club announced the arrival of Matias Fernandez-Pardo
fullText:
It was rather telling that Matias Fernandez-Pardo was Newcastle United's final signing of a rollercoaster summer.

This was a pursuit which was anything but straightforward.

The Belgian had been Newcastle's top target before the window opened, but it was only in the final stages of the summer that the club were able to complete a complex deal following delicate negotiations with Lille.

It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day.

On the same afternoon Newcastle announced the rapid Fernandez-Pardo's arrival, towering club-record signing Nick Woltemade finalised his loan move to Juventus.

Woltemade only joined Newcastle last summer, but this has been a window of change on Tyneside.

Head coach Eddie Howe stepped down in July and was replaced by Matthias Jaissle just a few weeks before the start of the new campaign.

Captain Bruno Guimaraes was among a handful of key players to leave while eight new signings arrived as Newcastle's records for spending and sales in a single window were both smashed.

This was the summer which altered the face of the club.

A shake-up had been signposted as far back as the spring.

It was in early April when Newcastle announced that defender Kieran Trippier would be leaving at the end of his contract.

The 34-year-old was approaching the twilight of his career, but his departure was still keenly felt as an influential figure behind the scenes.

"It was emotional for me, of course, because I loved the club so much and Newcastle gave me so much in return," the former England international said several months after moving on to Wolves.

"I'll always follow the club and want them to do well but, as a footballer, sometimes, you have to move on. With the utmost respect, I think it was the right time for both the club and myself.

"As I've always said, I wanted to leave in the right manner and show respect to my team-mates, the club and, most importantly, the supporters, who I have a great relationship with."

Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali's subsequent exits to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively did not necessarily come as a surprise, either, given they enabled Newcastle to comply and reinvest within the game's financial rules.

No-one internally had countenanced losing talisman Guimaraes, though.

However, having bailed Newcastle out so many times before, even the tireless midfielder dropped to the turf, untied his boots before the physio reached him and glared at the bench to come off during last season's final-day defeat at Fulham.

If ever an image summed up a bruising domestic campaign as Newcastle finished in 12th place - far below where the hierarchy had projected - and missed out on millions worth of European revenue.

The prospect of Guimaraes signing a new deal was unsurprisingly shot down by a figure involved in his subsequent £75m move to Arsenal a few weeks later.

After losing Alexander Isak to Liverpool against their wishes last summer, Newcastle ended up selling a fourth key player in less than a year.

They also missed out on top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi, who opted to move to Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.

Yet those inside the club repeatedly stressed that the window could only be judged once it shut.

"Just because one element doesn't go the way you want doesn't mean you abandon the plan," a senior source said.

"We stayed on target, stayed focused, stayed calm and moved on. We didn't do a whole lot of mourning or crying when we had a setback.

The final fortnight of the summer ultimately proved critical as defender Amar Dedic, midfielder Nico Gonzalez and forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo all joined the club.

Season ticket holder Adam Widdrington believes the trio's arrivals and Newcastle's performances in the 2-2 draw against Liverpool and the 2-0 win at Tottenham Hotspur changed the narrative.

"Plenty of pundits and other fans had Newcastle earmarked for relegation," he said.

"They said, 'Who's the manager? Never heard of him. Who are these young players? You have lost a load of players'.

"I still wouldn't class it as a great transfer window, but I think it's a good one, especially given the context of where it looked like Newcastle were heading in that Bruno dip.

"At that point, it didn't feel like there was so much to inspire the fans, but the last three signings shifted opinion a lot."

Fernandez-Pardo certainly feels more of a stylistic fit for a side who made the most sprints in the opening weekend (138) of the Premier League season.

Jaissle has already cited the forward's "explosiveness" which, for all his endeavour, was not part of Woltemade's game, even during an impressive start to his Newcastle career a year ago.

Fernandez-Pardo will have to quickly adapt and there will inevitably be ups and downs as the campaign progresses for the 21-year-old and a young side.

"We always have hope and belief," Jaissle said before a ball had even been kicked this season. "No one can take that away from us."

fullText:
PlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Bit Reactor
Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM

Even if you’re unfamiliar with the term “emergent storytelling”, you’ve likely experienced some of the unscripted tales that can bubble up out of a game’s systems. Perhaps you’ve led a scheming dynasty in Crusader Kings, or watched a favourite hero succumb to madness in Darkest Dungeon. Maybe you’ve surrendered yourself to the infinite yarn-spinner that is Dwarf Fortress – or read about it from the mid-00s forums where users helped popularise the term “Let’s Play” by chronicling their games in descriptive posts. Or perhaps you’ve played Firaxis’ XCOM, the alien invasion tactics hit that several key members of Zero Company studio Bit Reactor had a hand in.

Zero Company hinges on a concept as simple as it is perfect: take the complementary class abilities, tough dice rolls, and permanent character deaths of XCOM, and house them in a sci-fi setting known for spaghetti western blaster duels, last stands and heroic sacrifices. As creative director Greg Foertsch puts it, “Star Wars is about loss.” Which losses you end up mourning in Zero Company depends on you.

In theory, anyway. The game echoes Rogue One in its titular company of doomed misfits, but despite selling permadeath as a looming threat in the scripted tutorial, things rarely get dicey enough to put your squad in real danger. Even on its toughest difficulty, Zero Company feels reluctant to let a stray thermal detonator cut your companions’ stories short, blunting much of its potential for unscripted drama.

But in lieu of heroic sacrifices, Zcom (as I like to call it) is exceptional at telling a different kind of emergent story. Ones about iron-clad camaraderie and uneasy alliances. About the time your Mandalorian medic jetted in to heal your Jedi right on time, or the begrudging “nice shot” your clone trooper paid a former enemy sniper. The script feels designed to sell your mercenaries as an inseparable, dysfunctional family. Unironically, this one really is about the friends you make along the way.

Each fight is a reminder that Zero Company have each other’s backs. After an opening shot at enemy droids, you might have Kabb – a squat, bulbous alien scoundrel who speaks entirely in cutesy anastrophes – rush over and punch a hulking robot straight down a ravine. “What’s for supper? Cutty-upper!”, he declares for the third time in 15 minutes, met by some variations of “nicely done” from a random squadmate. Kabb’s still in bad shape from last turn, so you have your Astromech launch over healing stim. Kabb grabs it mid-air, slams it into his bicep, thanks the droid, and a notification tells you their bond has gotten stronger. That’ll mean a nice stat bump for them both later.

As all this happens, the battlefield buzzes with noise and motion. Idle combatants trade harmless potshots, ducking behind cover. Blaster holes sizzle through steel barriers. Battle Droids mock your missed shots, babbling “oh no!” like exploding lemmings when their comrades fall. There is so much personality in the different ways characters move. Gangers scramble down ladders. Astromechs bump into crates, then jump-jet over. Jedi leap and flip, and droids curl and spin like chrome woodlice. Through it all, veteran Star Wars composer Gordy Haab underscores every peril and triumph, paying pitch-perfect tribute to the textures of John Williams’ original score.

Between missions, you’ll return to the Den: a streamlined but engaging take on the customisation and upgrades of XCOM’s command centre, with the hangout space of Mass Effect’s Normandy. Via a galaxy map, you’ll spend intel, collect rewards, and make tough choices about which upgrades to deny your foes. It’s also here you’ll learn about your crew’s pasts. If you’ve got the time, you can even join them on personal quests.

I haven’t mentioned Zero Company’s overarching plot so far, mainly because there’s little worth mentioning. Its central threat, the Infinite Coil, are a tiresomely exoticised, first-draft cult with ill-defined goals, evidently concocted because the combat needed an enemy faction with some flavour of space magic for variety’s sake. The enemy’s reliance on healing and damage negation – a clumsy workaround for AI that can’t keep up with your team’s escalating stats and skills – results in some laborious late-game encounters.

These are by far the weakest parts of an otherwise brilliant debut from Bit Reactor, however. And even when the plot falters, touching character moments join digestible, deeply human explorations of this era of Star Wars’ byzantine factional politics. XCOM’s success has influenced countless turn-based tactics games. Few have made squeezing joyfully absurd heroics out of a handful of action points feel this good. Fewer have made me grin so hard at a final lucky shot during a last-second evacuation. That’s my squad down there, after all.

Star Wars: Zero Company is out now: £39.99

The same week union members at the University of Sydney agreed to a 24-hour strike, staff received the results of an internal survey.

In the faculty of arts and social sciences, 0% agreed with the statement: “I trust the University of Sydney to act in the best interests of staff, students and the broader community.”

It was the issue of trust, alongside longstanding concerns over staff protections from artificial intelligence, workload fairness and job security, that saw about 2,000 members to walk off the job on Wednesday.

From 7am, about 500 people were stationed at picket lines at each of the inner Sydney campus’s entrances, armed with flags, banners and megaphones.

The University of Sydney advised students “almost all” scheduled classes would move online as a result of the strike, while others were rescheduled or cancelled.

Peter Chen, the branch president of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) at the University of Sydney, said management had rebuffed the union “at every opportunity” to enforce appropriate protections around the use of AI.

“Higher education is the canary in the coalmine,” he said. “Where we go on AI … will travel through the rest of the economy.”

The New South Wales division secretary of the NTEU, Vince Caughley, said the University of Sydney’s own green paper advised AI was the most “fundamental transformation” education had seen, pointing to AI chatbots that were already being used to help teach online-only classes at other universities.

“We are asking for best practice, we are asking for due diligence,” he said. “Not their own commercialisation aims and certainly not the interest of venture capital.”

The union was confident it would reach an agreement with management within the year but had concerns over the lack of senior leadership at the table, including the provost, Prof Annamarie Jagose. The last bargaining process represented the longest running industrial action at an Australian university, and the prospect of future strikes remained active.

A spokesperson for the University of Sydney said it was “continuing to engage” with the union and maintained industrial action was “premature”.

“We agree using AI ethically requires a human-centred approach, and our … principles and guardrails that govern use have been developed in consultation with our community,” they said.

“We support many of the objectives of the unions’ claims, but believe it’s more appropriate to implement many of these through relevant policies, instead of in the Enterprise Agreement.”

There are broader concerns, some interlinked and widespread in the sector. Growing class sizes and reduced student satisfaction. A new proposal for teaching-only roles with no research component or scope for future growth.

Prof Laura Shepherd in the school of social and political sciences is part of the bargaining team and said students often sacrificed a “huge amount” to come to the university, including spending $50,000 on degrees.

“They come here … for quality and access to research leaders,” she said. “I think we should be very ashamed if we allow anything in the enterprise agreement that threatens that.”

The University of Sydney’s NTEU branch is the largest in Australia, and the university has long been a hotbed for activism. As management approaches its fifth month of bargaining, it is also grappling with continued opposition to its response to Gaza and restrictions on protest.

New restrictions were brought in as a result of the university’s pro-Palestine encampment in 2024, which received intense scrutiny during this year’s royal commission. On Wednesday, keffiyehs and pro-Palestine banners stood out among purple NTEU flags and signage.

The Student Representative Council was also striking in solidarity with staff and picketing online classes. Its education officer, Dana Kafina, said the university’s “draconian” protest restrictions were a motivation.

“In the wake of … suppressions of free speech and activism, and some of the lowest rates of student and graduate satisfaction in the country, we have had enough,” she said.

Despite the presence of campus security and police, the picket lines had a jovial atmosphere. Some blasted music on speakers, others banged drums and chanted with abandon.

Kurt Iveson, a professor of geography, was among them, running a quiz on his megaphone as, behind him, students sold baked goods to raise funds for lost income of strikers.

Iveson has been with the university for 20 years, and wants “meaningful protections” that do not outlaw AI but ensure “the tech is serving our purpose, rather than us serving the tech”.

“All of us on the picket line today are here because we care so much about the education and research we do,” he said.

SERV is an award-winning bit-serial RISC-V core

In fact, the award-winning SERV is the world's smallest RISC-V CPU. It's the perfect companion whenever you need a bit of computation and silicon real estate is at a premium.

How small is it then? Synthesizing the latest version of SERV in its most minimal form, yields the following results for some popular FPGA architectures and a typical CMOS process.

SERV is open source released under the ISC license. If you need a commercial license with patent grants, professional paid support or added features, please contact olof@award-winning.me

Don't feed serv any illegal instructions after midnight. Many logic expressions are hand-optimized using the old-fashioned method with Karnaugh maps on paper, and shamelessly take advantage of the fact that some opcodes aren't supposed to appear.
