title: SoulAuth – Rust identity infrastructure for humans and AI agents
description: Contribute to TrantorLabs/SoulAuth development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
Actor-native identity infrastructure for Human and AIActor subjects.

SoulAuth is open-source identity and authentication infrastructure built by
TRANTOR LABS, Singapore. It is written in Rust, supports self-hosting and OpenID
Connect, can serve Web, Backend, API and AI / Agent systems on its own, and integrates
natively with SoulseedOS.

中文版本见 README.zh-CN.md。
Full documentation: https://soulauth.trantorlabs.sg/

Traditional identity systems assume the subject is a Human User; a bot, service account
or agent is a special object hanging off a human account or an application. As AI moves
from a one-shot call towards an Actor that keeps understanding, judging, calling tools
and taking part in real-world action, a more basic question surfaces:

SoulAuth starts from that question and puts Actor Identity at the centre of the
identity model. Human and AIActor can both be first-class subjects; they may hold
different credentials, authentication methods and lifecycles, but they enter the same
Actor-native identity contract.

First-class standing for Human and AIActor does not mean the two share credentials,
capabilities, lifecycles, permissions or legal status. It means each can independently
be a subject that is identifiable, authenticable, able to establish an AuthSession, able
to be expressed through a token, and attributable in the audit trail.

Actor Identity is the identity root; a credential is how a subject proves itself.
A human can use a password, MFA or an external identity; an AIActor uses a key-based
credential suited to a machine subject. The paths converge on one authentication core
and produce a standardised authenticated identity and claims.

SoulAuth proves who an Actor is. It does not grant that Actor any power to act just
because authentication succeeded. In a Soulseed environment the AIActor itself is
defined by SoulseedAGI; SoulAuth authenticates that subject through a controlled
Canonical Actor Binding, and never defines, modifies or owns its Mind.

Large language models already provide increasingly strong generation, understanding,
reasoning and tool use. We prefer to read an LLM as the general compute of the
intelligence era, something like a CPU: it supplies intelligence, but it does not by
itself produce the identity, continuity, accountability and governance order that a
long-lived intelligent system needs.

Once AI stops being a single call and becomes a continuously existing Actor, the system
has to answer, reliably: who is understanding, who is judging, who is acting, and to
whom the result belongs.

That is why SoulAuth is Actor First. Before memory, knowledge, judgment, action and
accountability, establish a stable who.

So SoulAuth does not keep the traditional User as the root of every identity object,
and it is not a type = ai column added to a user table. A few boundaries hold
throughout:

Human Account, Identity Binding, Credential and Client each have their own
responsibility, and none of them can stand in for Actor Identity.

SoulAuth runs on its own, but it is not an isolated thought project. It is also part of
TRANTOR LABS' answer to the question of AGI infrastructure.

Our reading is this: if the LLM supplies the intelligence, a system built for long-lived
AIActors still needs a Mind above it, continuous operation, governance, applications,
and the order required to enter public reality.

The infrastructure divides into four layers of responsibility.

SoulseedAGI — the mind kernel defines the AIActor and its continuous Mind.

SoulseedOS — the runtime and governance operating system keeps that Mind running
continuously, safely and under governance.

Soulseed Apps — the application layer turns Mind and operating-system capability
into real applications.

Public Reality Infrastructure carries the public facts and trust that must be
verifiable across subjects.

SoulAuth occupies the identity-infrastructure position in this stack. It is not a part
of SoulseedAGI and not an internal module of SoulseedOS. It keeps its own boundary: it
can be composed by SoulseedOS, and it can serve entirely different systems on its own.

SoulseedAGI defines the subject and its Mind, SoulAuth authenticates the subject,
SoulseedOS runs and governs it.

SoulAuth's boundary ends at a trustworthy identity fact.

SoulAuth does not define a Mind and does not stand in for a higher governance system.
A successful authentication does not by itself produce a mandate, a business permission,
a governance decision, a lease, or the right to act in the real world.

The shortest form of the boundary:

Identity answers "who", authority answers "why this Actor may act here and now".

SoulAuth ships a small RBAC model, but that model governs SoulAuth's own admin surface
only. Every permission it defines is namespaced soulauth: for exactly this reason —
a consuming system may well have its own users.read, and the two are different things
that happen to share a name. A role granted here is a claim about the account, never
an authorization decision inside the consumer. See
Using SoulAuth as an OIDC provider.

SoulAuth takes Actor Identity as the identity root and separates Human Account,
Identity Binding and Credential. Credentials enter the authentication core to establish
a trustworthy identity fact, AuthSession carries authentication continuity, and
Token & Federation then hands that fact to external consumers as tokens, OIDC, SSO
and claims.

Control Plane, Security Protection and Audit & Attribution cut across the whole
identity lifecycle; Persistence & Infrastructure underneath provides the data, keys,
external IdPs and adapters that bound the runtime.

The figure shows logical responsibilities, not a call sequence and not a deployment
diagram — everything in it runs in one process today. SoulAuth can keep a small
operational surface by default, a Rust service and a SurrealDB. A simple physical
deployment does not license mixing the domains inside it:

Identity, Credential, AuthSession, OIDC, Security and Audit still have distinct logical
sources, lifecycles and responsibility boundaries even when one database carries them
all.

Standalone. SoulAuth can act as an independent identity provider for conventional
Web, Backend, API and AI / Agent systems, offering complete identity capability through
authentication, AuthSession, OIDC, tokens and claims.

Within Soulseed. SoulAuth supplies SoulseedOS with authenticated Actor identity
facts through a stable adapter. For a canonical AIActor already defined by SoulseedAGI,
SoulAuth maintains a controlled identity binding, and never reads, modifies or owns its
Mind.

Both use the same SoulAuth core. Soulseed is the native integration direction, not a
precondition for using SoulAuth.

Identity infrastructure needs explicit data ownership, strong type boundaries, memory
safety and predictable system behaviour. We want Identity, Credential, AuthSession and
the other security boundaries to exist not only in the architecture documents, but as
constraints the code itself finds hard to violate.

Security and audit are not peripheral capabilities added once SoulAuth is deployed;
they are part of the identity infrastructure itself. Credential, Authentication,
AuthSession, Token, Key, External IdP and audit integrity are all treated as explicit
security boundaries, with continuous protection built around MFA, lockout, replay
protection, token reuse detection, key lifecycle and tamper-evident audit.

The concrete posture is in Security posture below; the reporting
path for vulnerabilities is in SECURITY.md.

Everything from here on is operational: how to run it, what it exposes, how it is
tested, and where it is still incomplete.

Requires a running SurrealDB and a Rust toolchain (edition 2021).

APP_URL is the public address, not the listen address (that is BIND_ADDR,
default 0.0.0.0:8080). It determines the OIDC issuer, the prefix of links in
outgoing mail, and whether session cookies carry Secure.

Pointing APP_URL at a non-loopback host switches on the production gates —
see Security posture and
DEPLOYMENT.md.

There is no default account. A fresh instance prints a one-time token in its startup log
(at WARN, so it is visible at the default level); use it to create the first
administrator without touching the database:

The gate closes permanently once an administrator exists, and returns the same response
for a wrong token as for a closed gate.

Every endpoint returns the resource itself — there is no {success, data, message}
envelope. Actions that produce no resource answer 204 No Content.

The OIDC endpoints (/.well-known/openid-configuration, /jwks, /token,
/userinfo, /authorize) return the shapes their specs mandate — including
{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"…"} on the token endpoint.
That is the one deliberate exception: wrapping them would break every standard
OIDC client library.

85 operations over 72 paths. contracts/openapi.yaml is the authoritative list and
tests/conformance.rs::j4 holds it against the route table in both directions; this is
the shape of it.

Every endpoint is exercised by the integration suite. Representative flows:

The decisions below are the ones worth knowing before you deploy, because each
of them is a place where the obvious implementation is wrong in a way that does
not announce itself.

Sensitive endpoints — login, registration, password reset, email verification —
share their counters through the database. Without that, an N-replica
deployment hands an attacker N times the allowance.

The general API limit stays in-process: putting a database round-trip on the hot
path would make the limiter the bottleneck. The line is self-maintaining —
anything registered with an explicit endpoint rule gets shared counting.

One consequence worth internalising: restarting a replica no longer clears a
quota. That is the point (a restart must not work as a jailbreak), but it
surprises people during incident response.

Two layers with different jobs. Neither substitutes for the other.

Unit tests cover pure logic and consistency invariants — permission names
matching the seed data, endpoint path shapes, configuration validation, token
claim construction.

Integration tests run a real SurrealDB, a real service process, and two
dependency-free stand-ins (tests/smtp_sink.py receives mail,
tests/mock_oauth.py plays Google and GitHub). They assert contract-level
behaviour that compiles fine when broken:

Useful switches: KEEP_WORK=1 preserves logs, mailbox and the last response
body; ports are overridable via SURREAL_PORT / APP_PORT / SINK_PORT /
OAUTH_PORT / APP2_PORT.

The same instance serves standalone use and provider use — there is no mode
switch. A consuming system is simply another registered client.

The division of labour is the part that gets misconfigured:

Two consequences that cost debugging time when missed:

Registration, the exact parameters a consumer needs, and three behaviours an
integrator cannot discover without reading the source are documented under
Register a client and
OIDC and clients.

Four variables are required: JWT_SECRET, APP_URL, SMTP_HOST, SMTP_FROM.
Everything else has a default or is genuinely optional — including both OAuth
providers.

The full table and the production gates are in DEPLOYMENT.md.
Reverse-proxy and multi-replica notes, and a troubleshooting index organised by
symptom that points the wrong way, are on the documentation site:
Deployment and
Troubleshooting.

Deployment steps live in DEPLOYMENT.md — that file is what
tests/deployment_walkthrough.sh executes on every push.

SoulAuth's goal is not to lock identity capability inside one application, model or
ecosystem. It aims to be identity infrastructure that can be deployed independently,
rests on open standards, and composes with other systems through a stable contract. A
consumer should never need to read SoulAuth's private database, nor depend on its
internal implementation, to use it correctly.

SoulAuth is built by TRANTOR LABS, Singapore. What TRANTOR LABS works on is not a
single AI product but the more basic question of the AGI era: once intelligence becomes

title: What should you look out for this Premiership midweek?
description: With five games on Wednesday and an Edinburgh derby on Thursday, plus a transfer deadline looming, what should you look out for in the Scottish Premiership this midweek?
fullText:
Only a handful of games into the Scottish Premiership season and it could be argued that about half its team managers are already looking nervously over their shoulders.

At least most do not have to deal with a transfer deadline day before preparing for this midweek's fixtures as the domestic deadline has been delayed until the dust had settled on the five games scheduled for Wednesday evening.

However, while they have another chance to assess their reshaped squads before another hasty round of phone calls and negotiations before the transfer window closes at 17:00 BST on Thursday, Heart of Midlothian and Hibernian have no such luxury as they meet later that evening.

So what should we look out for in that big game - and the five others on Wednesday?

What are big questions in final two days of Scottish transfer window?

Why is Scotland's transfer window closing on Thursday?

Celtic sign Parma's Sorensen, with more to come before deadline

At the start of the campaign you would have imagined there would be no question marks about Martin O'Neill's position after he rescued a league and couple double out of a traumatic season in his second spell as Celtic's interim manager.

However, the veteran Northern Irishman missed last month's win over Kilmarnock after "a small medical procedure" in hospital then endured a 5-1 thrashing by LASK that meant Celtic again missed out on the riches of the Champions League.

Saturday's subsequent 2-1 home win over Falkirk was hardly convincing, adding to the doubts some supporters once again have voiced about their summer transfer dealings, and assistant Shaun Maloney was sent out to meet the media instead on Tuesday.

Neverthless, they have won all five of their games apart from that collapse in Austria and go into Wednesday's meeting with Aberdeen already two points clear at the top of the table.

Similarly, counterpart Stephen Robinson has still to convince some Dons fans despite steering them clear of relegation trouble last season then starting the season with six wins and just two losses.

To make matters worse, after Sunday's home defeat by Rangers, few will be expecting much from a trip to Celtic Park, where they have not won in 14 visits.

Indeed, Celtic won all three meetings last season after Aberdeen, who have not won in 15 away league games, edged the 2025 Scottish Cup final on penalties.

Steven Pressley was not a popular choice as Dundee head coach last season, but his subsequent charm offensive means he will be forgiven quickly for a defeat by Hibernian on Sunday that ended their six-game winning run at Dens Park.

Having admitted he failed to "find the right solutions" to thwart the Leith side, Pressley now must work out how to beat St Johnstone for the first time as a manager, having lost all three meetings with the Perth side when Falkirk manager in season 2009-10.

However, other statistics are in his favour, with St Johnstone having only won one of their latest 10 meetings and Simo Valakari's side having lost three in a row on the road after Saturday's loss to Hearts and winning just one of their latest five outings overall.

Given Saturday's 4-0 home drubbing by Dundee United, it is hard to argue that Neil McCann is not the manager most under pressure.

That came after a 5-1 thrashing by Celtic in their last home league game.

A 3-2 Ayrshire derby win over second-tier Ayr United came in between that, but that is their only victory in five outings.

McCann will take heart from two wins over St Mirren since taking charge in January, a 4-3 victory at Rugby Park in February then a 3-0 success in Paisley in May.

It leaves Kilmarnock unbeaten in four meetings with the Buddies since losing on penalties in League Cup last September after 2-2 draw in Ayrshire.

Craig McLeish's side arrive having been held to a 3-3 draw by Motherwell on Sunday after a 5-1 hammering by Rangers in the League Cup.

However, until then, St Mirren had been unbeaten in five away from home, winning the latest three without conceding a goal, and will be out to prove the Ibrox capitulation was a mere blip.

Having continued the swashbuckling style imposed successfully by Jens Berthel Askou last season, Motherwell's Alfred Johansson is probably the manager least under scrutiny.

Yet the Swede's side are without a win in four after Sunday's draw with St Mirren and are also four trips away from home without a win, albeit two of those were in Conference League qualifying against HJK Helsinki and Freiburg.

Indeed, they have lost 10 goals in their latest three outings and, including the end of last season under his predecessor, they have gone five home league games without a win.

Jim Goodwin will have had a wry smile from his hospital bed considering his United side had gone three games without scoring before crushing Kilmarnock on Saturday to end run of four without a win and three straight defeats in his absence.

They also failed to score in two defeats and one draw with Well last season, losing 2-0 twice at Fir Park - and have lost all five visits since a win in April 2023.

Goodwin will hope they can alter that trend too under assistant Sharp on Wednesday.

Rangers have only lost one of their latest five outings, but amid those results they failed to qualify for either the Europa League or the Conference League.

So Sunday's win over Aberdeen, albeit it narrow, has eased some of the pressure building early into Derek McInnes' Rangers reign.

It will be lumped back on again should they fail to beat Falkirk considering John McGlynn's side are without a win in three and have lost four of their past five at home, including their latest three in the league.

Included among those are a 5-2 hammering by Rangers on the final weekend of last season, a near repeat of the 6-3 scoreline on their previous visit, leaving the Ibrox side unbeaten in six meetings since Falkirk won 3-2 in Championship in March 2016.

Both capital clubs impressed in Conference League play-offs on Thursday, albeit Hibs ultimately lost out to two late goals at home to Gent.

David Gray's side bounced back with a 2-1 win away to Dundee that means they have suffered just one defeat in their latest seven outings.

Hearts followed up their European heroics against Rapid Vienna by holding off a spirited St Johnstone comeback on Sunday and are now unbeaten in six since a 6-1 thrashing by Benfica completed an opening four defeats under new head coach Wouter Vrancken.

A 2-1 derby victory against nine men at Easter Road in April is, nevertheless, Hearts' only win in eight league games on the road.

Should they win a third derby in a row, they will have consigned Hibs to five straight home league defeats for the first time since 2010. Some incentive!

Celtic could introduce their latest signing, Oliver Sorensen on loan from Parma, but he will surely not replace Benjamin Nygren in midfield considering the Swede scored in all three of their games against Aberdeen last season.

Two Scottish midfielders who have not quite lived up to their early promise could get their chance to revive their careers in opposition at Fir Park.

Former Dundee midfielder Lyall Cameron, whose family are United fans, could make his debut for the Tannadice side on loan from Rangers.

Meanwhile, Dylan Levitt will be keen to face his former club after his arrival from Leyton Orient.

United will also have to keep on eye on Tawanda Maswanhise, with last season's top scorer getting off the mark on Sunday and having already scored five times in six Premiership appearances against the Tannadice side, including three in his last two at Fir Park.

Former Kilmarnock defender Joe Wright could face St Johnstone after his move from Bradford City to Dundee, who might also complete the signing of Manchester United midfielder Jack Moorhouse in time to play.

Meanwhile, St Johnstone are hoping to gain permission to play former Fortuna Dusseldorf midfielder Danny Schmidt.

title: Keith credits training partners for 'saving my life'
description: Former Down hurler Stephen Keith credits the quick actions of his training partners after suffering a cardiac arrest in a gym.
fullText:
A former Down hurler who suffered a cardiac arrest in a gym says he would not be alive today without the quick actions of his training partners.

Stephen Keith collapsed after a training session at a gym in Portaferry and spent almost a month in Belfast's Royal Victoria Hospital as doctors worked to determine what had caused the cardiac arrest.

Reflecting on the incident, he said he considers himself "extremely lucky" to have survived and is now urging more people to learn CPR and ensure defibrillators are available in their communities.

"Wednesday morning I was in the gym, just a normal morning," the 39-year-old told BBC Sport NI.

"At the end of the class there was a finisher, more or less a race. After we finished it, I came off the bike and hit the ground."

He has little memory of what happened next, but friends told him he collapsed suddenly after walking away from the exercise bike and stopped breathing.

A trained nurse who was taking part in the session immediately began CPR, while others rushed to retrieve nearby defibrillators in the town.

"The downtime was about 20 to 22 minutes," he said.

"Without Barry (Milligan) being there and starting CPR, it wasn't looking good that morning. I was very, very lucky."

The former county hurler said the experience highlighted just how vital CPR training and access to defibrillators can be.

"I'm proof that it is life-saving," Keith told BBC Sport NI.

"If the lads weren't in the gym with me that morning and there wasn't a defib close by, I wouldn't be sitting here talking to you today. That's 100% true."

Doctors later discovered one of his main coronary arteries was blocked and inserted a stent. He has also had an implantable defibrillator fitted as a precaution.

While he has now been cleared to return to training and gym work, Keith, who was a goalkeeper for Down, believes his playing days are over.

"I've had a good career and a good run.

"I played county hurling up until last season and I was hoping to give another year to my club Ballycran. But personally, going forward, I don't think I will play again. I don't think it would be fair putting my wife and family through that."

The father of two says the incident has given him a new outlook on life.

"I have a five-year-old and a three-year-old at home. I just think to myself how lucky I am to have another chance here. I could have been dead, gone, and still had a wife and two young kids there."

Now, he hopes sharing his story will encourage others to learn CPR and support the provision of defibrillators.

"The main reason I'm telling this story is that CPR training saves lives.

"Communities, sports clubs and organisations need defibs and they need to make sure they're working - it saved my life."

title: Paredes puts question mark over Argentina future
description: Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes says it is going to be "difficult" for him to continue playing for his country in the wake of his 10-match international ban.
fullText:
Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes says it is going to be "difficult" for him to continue playing for his country in the wake of his 10-match international ban.

Paredes received the suspension from Fifa for his part in an on-pitch confrontation following Argentina's 1-0 defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.

The 32-year-old grabbed Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat and wrestled Gavi to the ground, before appearing to strike the latter in the face.

Paredes also suggested Argentina legend Lionel Messi retiring from international football could play a part in his decision.

"It's going to be difficult for me to stay with the national team," said Boca Juniors player Paredes.

"Because of the suspension as well, because of Leo's decision. It's going to be difficult for everything to carry on as before.

"I haven't discussed it with the coach [Lionel Scaloni] yet, but we'll talk about it and see what decision I make."

Argentina's Paredes banned for 10 games

Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give'

Messi, 39, recently announced his retirement from international football, saying he had "nothing left to give" having "given it my all".

He captained Argentina to World Cup glory in Qatar in 2022 but could not repeat the feat against Spain in his final game for his country.

Messi scored 125 goals in 207 appearances for Argentina to become his country's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player.

"Leo's legacy will live on forever because of what he achieved, for never giving up and for showing that dreams are hard-won, pursued and, in the end, fulfilled," Paredes added.

"We'd spoken in the final days of the World Cup about how the final would surely be his last match, but even so, we weren't prepared for that because of what he means to us."

fullText:
Aline Pereira is set to fight for a UFC contract that would see her join her brother and two-weight UFC champion Alex Pereira in the MMA promotion.

Aline will fight undefeated prospect Smilla Sundell, a Muay Thai champion in the Asia-based ONE Championship, on Dana White's Contender Series in Las Vegas on 13 October.

UFC president White's Contender Series offers a chance for fighters outside the UFC to win contracts in one-off contests.

Pereira, who currently holds a 3-2 record, with all three of her victories coming by decision, confirmed on her Instagram she will face Sweden's Sundell in a bantamweight bout.

The 35-year-old's most recent victory was a split decision against Jade Masson-Wong in May, on the undercard of Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions's first MMA event.

Several siblings have fought in the UFC together, including Nick and Nate Diaz, but a sister-brother duo is more rare.

Just like her brother, Pereira enjoyed a successful kickboxing career.

Her fights included a super-bantamweight title opportunity with Glory promotions, before she transitioned to MMA in 2022.

Pereira decided to step away from the sport in 2023 after her MMA career began with a rocky 1‑2 spell with Legacy Fighting Alliance (LFA).

She found momentum in Karate Combat League, going 3‑0 with two knockouts and winning the promotion's inaugural women's flyweight title in 2024.

The Brazilian returned to MMA in late 2025 and is often seen being trained and cornered by her brother, Alex.

Alex failed in his bid to become a three-weight UFC champion in June, losing to Frenchman Ciryl Gane in an interim heavyweight title fight.

Aline faces a tough opponent in Sundell, who has two wins in her MMA career to date.

title: Monfils wins on 40th birthday as Zverev celebrates at 2am
description: French veteran Gael Monfils is treated to a rendition of Happy Birthday by the US Open crowd as he becomes the oldest man to win a match there since 1992.
fullText:
Most people celebrate their 40th birthday with a slap-up meal or a surprise party.

Gael Monfils, the maverick Frenchman who always knows how to have fun on the court, marked his milestone by winning a Grand Slam match at the US Open.

Playing in the final major of his career, Monfils ensured he had a unforgettable night with a 2-6 6-1 6-2 6-0 victory over Paraguayan opponent Adolfo Daniel Vallejo.

The former world number six is the oldest man to win a US Open main-draw match since Jimmy Connors - who also won on his 40th birthday in 1992.

The New York crowd made the occasion even more memorable for Monfils by bursting into an impromptu rendition of Happy Birthday during his post-victory interview.

"To play on my 40th birthday is very special," said the 2016 US Open semi-finalist, who announced last year he will retire at the end of this season.

"The atmosphere [in New York] is always electric - I feel great here. I always try to play great tennis and put on a great show."

Addressing the thousands of fans who created a celebratory atmosphere on Louis Armstrong Stadium, he added: "You guys rock - let's keep it up for the second round."

No repeat of Wimbledon heroics as Fery exits US Open

Gauff's flaw forgotten on winning US Open return

Rybakina makes winning start in race to number one

Playing in his 18th and final US Open, Monfils made a nervous start against 60th-ranked Vallejo.

However, he quickly settled into the match and dominated the next three sets to secure a 131st Grand Slam match win - extending his all-time record for a Frenchman.

It was a typically entertaining display from the charismatic Monfils, who enthralled the crowd with the stylish shot-making and athleticism for which he is known.

"I didn't want to lose first round, that's for sure," said Monfils, who revealed he was given a watch by his wife Elina Svitolina - the two-time Wimbledon semi-finalist - as a birthday present.

"Somehow I felt like even with a sloppy start, I could do better. I kept going for my shots, being versatile with my backhand, tried to use my forehand.

"My rhythm was there and then I had this feeling where I can be in cruise control."

Monfils will continue his farewell appearance at Flushing Meadows against American 14th seed Learner Tien.

One man also left celebrating in the early hours of the New York morning was top seed Alexander Zverev.

The 29-year-old German survived a huge scare against Italy's Lorenzo Sonego to win a five-set thriller at almost 2am on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Zverev is aiming to reach the final for the third successive Grand Slam, but almost fell at the first hurdle after being pushed to the limit by 89th-ranked Sonego for almost five hours.

Sonego, 31, produced a stunning performance to lead by two sets to one - and was two points away from victory in the fourth set.

But Zverev, who won the first major of his career at the French Open before reaching the Wimbledon final, showed great resolve to escape with a 6-4 3-6 6-7 (7-9) 7-5 6-4 victory.

"I'm just happy I won - that's it," said Zverev.

"It was an incredible battle with ups and downs. I think it's the longest first round match I've ever played in my life.

"He played amazing tennis and would have beaten a lot of players for sure."

With world number one Jannik Sinner missing through injury, 29-year-old Zverev leads the seedings at a major for the first time in his career.

His prospects also appear to have been aided by Spanish second seed Carlos Alcaraz's lack of match practice following a long-term wrist injury, as well as 24-time major champion Novak Djokovic's own first-round exit on Sunday.

But with that increased sense of opportunity seemed to come edginess against Sonego.

Zverev, who suffered early exits in Montreal and Cincinnati leading into the US Open, was well below his best again as Sonego threatened to further blow open the men's singles draw.

"This was exactly the sort of match I needed," said Zverev, who goes on to play France's Quentin Halys in the second round.

"I struggled in the last two tournaments, I didn't play well and sometimes good things happen after you fight through one of these matches."

title: Gauff's flaw forgotten on winning US Open return
description: At last year's US Open, Coco Gauff's serve left her practising in the rain and crying on court - now it is a potent weapon.
fullText:
The sight of a forlorn Coco Gauff hitting serves in the rain on the US Open practice courts became the defining image of her struggles last year.

The serving yips were undermining the two-time major champion's talent. Staying out in the persistent drizzle was a sign of how desperate she had become to iron out the major flaw in her game.

Twelve months on, the 22-year-old American has returned to the US Open with a rejuvenated service game - and it was the bedrock of her 6-3 6-4 win over Turkey's Zeynep Sonmez in the New York first round on Tuesday.

Gauff starting with a swift hold to love set the tone for a dominant first set, then used her opening shot to get her out of trouble when Sonmez threatened to go a break up in the second set.

"Now it's like I can look back a year on and think, 'Oh, wow, it's a big difference'," said Gauff, who is seeded fourth at Flushing Meadows this year.

"It feels good to come into a tournament feeling confident on that shot finally."

No repeat of Wimbledon heroics as Fery exits US Open

Rybakina makes winning start in race to number one

On the eve of her home Slam last year, Gauff decided to reshuffle her coaching team and hired biomechanics expert Gavin MacMillan - who helped four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka overcome serving troubles earlier in her career.

It was a drastic move. But one which Gauff felt was unavoidable after hitting a high amount of double faults at the preceding Cincinnati Open.

Tweaking technique heading into the US Open - where she receives frenzied attention - was always going to be a risk.

So it was no surprise when Gauff suffered a fourth-round exit in a tournament where she looked fraught throughout and was reduced to tears during matches.

"Obviously last year I knew all the eyes were going to be on the serve," Gauff said.

"Gavin is so great at what he does, I felt a lot of pressure to kind of prove that. It didn't really show within the first two weeks, which is normal."

That was then. Now Gauff possesses a serve which is a serious weapon - even though she still leaks some double faults.

Showing greater consistency on the toss, not throwing the ball too far in front and keeping her wrist straighter have been MacMillan's pointers for a more reliable serve.

It was a key factor in her charge to the Cincinnati Open title earlier this month.

Analysis from that tournament showed how Gauff is hitting closer to the line but still maintaining her serve speed - underlining a significant improvement in her accuracy.

Gauff now has full confidence her serve can be too hot for opponents to handle - and it showed immediately against Sonmez.

The opening game saw Gauff thump a 112mph ace down the middle, followed by an unreturned first serve and another ace, on her way to holding serve in less than 90 seconds.

Sonmez struggled to get balls into play whenever Gauff landed a first serve in the first set, with the world number four winning 93% of those points.

Gauff broke again for a 1-0 lead in the second set, but her serve was not as effective as Sonmez levelled at 2-2 and held three more break points for a 4-2 lead.

But a precise ace out wide and a 115mph unreturned first serve enabled Gauff to cling on in a game which you felt she would have lost a year ago.

The gutsy hold laid the platform for Gauff to immediately break for 4-3 before securing victory with another service game which displayed her belief.

Gauff hit a trio of unreturned first serves - all just under the 120mph mark, teeing up three match points as Sonmez buckled on the first after a short rally.

"Psychologically, I'm now going to go for the ace, or I know I can hit the serve and the return is probably not going to come back," said Gauff, who will play Spain's Paula Badosa or Australia's Daria Kasatkina in the second round.

"Last year I literally was like I hope I make it in. It's such a big difference knowing almost every serve I'm trying to basically hit 110, 115, 120mph if I can."

title: Woods to change plea after March's crash arrest
description: The golfer will be in court on Wednesday for a hearing to change his plea after being charged with driving under the influence.
fullText:
Tiger Woods is to change his plea in court five months after he was arrested on a charge of driving under the influence in a rollover crash in Florida.

Court records show the change of plea hearing is set for Wednesday morning in Martin County, Florida. The golfer was arrested after the March crash, and had passed a breathalyser test but declined further testing for other drugs.

He pleaded not guilty the same month to misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence and refusal to submit to testing. Woods, 50, said he was seeking treatment after the incident.

It was not immediately clear what the change of plea would be. The BBC has contacted prosecutors and Woods' attorney.

No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.

Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.

In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom".

He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.

Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning.

He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.

Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".

Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.

Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today.

"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."

The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

title: Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?
description: Arsenal have been busy in the transfer market as they look to defend their Premier League title, but do they lack a world class striker still?
fullText:
"Very ambitious, very fast, and very smart."

That was manager Mikel Arteta's aim for Arsenal's transfer dealings following their defeat by Paris St-Germain in the Champions League final in May.

The Gunners won their first title in 22 years last season by seven points and did not lose a game in the Champions League during normal time, with their only loss in the competition coming to Luis Enrique's side on penalties.

But it was clear coming into the summer transfer window that the club were looking for a game-changing attacker to lift their forward line.

Viktor Gyokeres - a £64m signing last summer from Portuguese side Sporting - scored 21 goals in his first season for Arsenal but his performances still raised questions about whether he is the best fit for Arteta's side going forward.

The same debate was posed on the left wing with Leandro Trossard's form dipping after starting the season well and Gabriel Martinelli, despite scoring six goals in the Champions League campaign, scoring just once in the league.

And now both of those players have left the club.

But finding an attacker who could elevate a squad that almost won a domestic and European double proved difficult.

Arsenal want to be one of the best clubs in the world.

In an interview with the Times, chief executive Richard Garlick said that joining the world's super-clubs is "the goal - that's the ambition".

In that same interview, Garlick acknowledged that the "pool of players is smaller now than it was a few years ago if we're going to improve".

And unfortunately for the Gunners, they have found that out this summer.

Sporting director Andrea Berta is known for speaking to multiple targets at once while preparing the deals simultaneously.

The Gunners went into this window with interest in Morgan Rogers, Bradley Barcola, Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr.

Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius Jr turned public and was shaped around his contract situation at Real Madrid.

Ultimately, the Spanish club offered him a bigger package than they had done before Arsenal's interest stepped up.

But inside the club, there was a period where they thought they were going to be successful in bringing one of the best wingers in world football to north London.

Questions will be posed as to why the club did not go big for Rogers, but Arsenal stuck to their valuation of £80m before Chelsea then paid £117m for the former Aston Villa forward.

That left Julian Alvarez as the only available target in the window after Liverpool succeeded in bringing in Bradley Barcola.

Arsenal always had reservations about paying the fee needed to get Barcola too.

It appeared Alvarez's only way out of Atletico Madrid was Arsenal, after Atleti were adamant that they would not negotiate with Barcelona.

However, Alvarez returned to training with the Spanish side and, despite Arteta's best efforts laying out plans to the player, the deal did not come off.

Arteta joins elite 250 club - but where does he rank?

Arsenal's Nwaneri joins Dortmund on loan

Arsenal showed the strength of their squad in their win over Aston Villa on Monday night.

They brought in Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes for £75m, Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa (£55m), turned Piero Hincapie's loan deal into a permanent one (£34.5m) and signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m.

Tzolis struggled in the win but has already impressed in the Community Shield victory over Manchester City and the opening day Premier League win over Coventry.

Guimaraes is being described by some as one of the signings of the window, and Konsa was statistically the best defender in the league for ground duel success (73.1%) and passing accuracy (95%) last season.

Konsa, although he brings the number of senior defenders in Arsenal's squad to eight, was brought in because of the injuries to William Saliba and Jurrien Timber.

A big part of Arsenal's window has been who they have let go too.

Gabriel Martinelli is close to completing a move for around £60m to Al-Hilal, which would be a record sale for the club.

Leandro Trossard has moved to Besiktas (£15.3m), while Christian Norgaard was sold to Everton (£7m).

The main worry from supporters is that they have let two forwards go who play on the left wing and brought in just one to replace them.

There is no denying that Arsenal wanted a game-changing attacker this summer - if there was one available.

Not signing one this window does leave them with the chance to act again in January or wait completely until next summer to try to bring in a new forward.

But there will be uncomfortable conversations about why there hasn't been one during this window, even if the football leadership team are content with the business the club has done.

Questions will of course be asked of Arteta, Berta and co-chair Josh Kroenke as to why, after Arsenal's success, such an attractive club weren't able to get one of their targets over the line.

However, there is no denying that Arsenal's squad is one of the best in Europe. Their bench for the win over Aston Villa contained nine full internationals with two of those - Merino and Zubimendi - World Cup winners.

Gabriel Jesus has moved to Barcelona for £12.8m, and although he was not an integral part of Arsenal's team because of selection and fitness issues, he still made 27 appearances in all competitions, scoring six goals.

With Martinelli and Trossard both gone, there will be more opportunity for Eberechi Eze to play from the left wing, a position he shone in at former club Crystal Palace.

Eze played in some of the biggest games of Arsenal's last campaign on the left wing and put in an impressive appearance in that role in the win over Villa on Monday too.

Last season, Kai Havertz missed large parts of the campaign with injury, while Mikel Merino, another option to play at striker, missed a chunk of the season too but both have started this season fully fit.

Those injuries last season meant that Gyokeres had to lead the line for long periods without back-up in his first campaign with Arsenal, but despite that test, it does not take away that the Swedish international's suitability is still in question.

It is also intriguing that Gyokeres has not played a minute of the opening two Premier League matches so far.

Arsenal are still looking like the early season favourites and have the potential to defend their title, but criticism surrounding the lack of a new forward will be tough to avoid if goals start to become hard to come by.

title: Russia economy could go ‘beserk’ with military-industrial complex, Putin envoy warns
description: Russia has hiked taxes, embarked on property redistribution, welcomed contributions from businesses to finance the war, and, most recently, threatened business owners who are not doing enough to protect their facilities from Ukrainian drones.
fullText:
MOSCOW (Reuters) - The Russian economy runs a risk of going "berserk" if it is run to focus entirely on the needs of the military-industrial complex, President Vladimir Putin's international development envoy was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

The comments by Boris Titov to business news outlet RBC were a rare sign of concern in Kremlin circles about the increasing pressure on the slowing economy to secure a victory in the 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine.

Titov, appointed in 2024 as Putin's special representative to international organizations for achieving sustainable development goals, is a wealthy businessman who used to own Russia's leading producer of sparkling wine. He led an influential business lobby and ran for president in 2018.

"Military and civilian economies have always existed in symbiosis everywhere. Many technical inventions that are useful for all originated within the military-industrial complex. The key lies in maintaining balance," Titov told RBC.

Russia has hiked taxes, embarked on property redistribution, welcomed contributions from businesses to finance the war, and, most recently, threatened business owners who are not doing enough to protect their facilities from Ukrainian drones.

War hawks and some government officials often refer to the reorganisation of the Soviet economy under dictator Josef Stalin during World War Two as a model, citing the wartime slogan "Everything for the front, everything for victory".

This approach is met with cautious but growing resistance from various sectors.

"This is not an economy at all, it's a kind of 'berserk mode' that can only exist for a very limited time, and the necessity of which should be considered very carefully," Titov said on the eve of a major economic forum that Putin will attend this week in Russia's Far East.

RBC, which conducted the interview, noted that the term berserk derived from mythological Norse warriors who entered a trance-like state, possibly drug-induced, that enabled them to fight ferociously and ignore pain.

The Russian economy is expected to grow at only 0.4% this year, and many non-military sectors are stagnating or shrinking. Ukrainian attacks on economic targets such as refineries, online retailers and oil and grain export infrastructure may push this growth rate even lower.

Titov's comments echo a statement by Moscow's technocrat mayor Sergei Sobyanin, who argued last month that "killing a normal economy is equivalent to killing the whole country".

title: Get ready to meet the 'love child' of the dot-com crash and financial crisis, tech guru Erik Gordon says
description: The AI boom marries the lofty valuations of the dot-com bubble with the contagion risks of the financial crisis, business professor Erik Gordon said.
fullText:
An AI slump will combine features of the dot-com crash and Great Financial Crisis, Erik Gordon says.

The business professor said the AI boom couples extreme valuations with enormous contagion risk.

Potential "losers" include banks, insurers, and investors in index funds and ETFs, Gordon said.

The AI boom marries dangerous elements of internet mania and the mid-2000s credit bubble, raising the specter of a financial catastrophe, Erik Gordon says.

"The next crash will look like the love child of the dot-com crash and the Great Financial Crisis," the entrepreneurship professor told Business Insider by email.

Gordon, who teaches at the University of Michigan's Ross School of Business, said the AI boom "inherited the hype and overvaluations of the dot-com bubble."

While the nascent technology is likely to create more value than the internet, he said, company valuations are so extreme that "most investors will get killed, just like most of the dot-com investors."

Gordon, who researches topics such as technology commercialization and AI, said the "losers" from an AI crash will extend beyond direct investors to buyers of index funds and exchange-traded funds, given that tech giants make up such a large part of the market.

The five largest US companies by market cap — Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon — are together valued at over $20 trillion, in no small part because investors expect them to be huge winners from the AI trend.

Gordon also raised the alarm on the scale of AI companies' debts. They've "racked up a few trillion dollars of debt obligations on and off their balance sheets, and they're not done borrowing," he said.

If they're unable to repay even a portion of their commitments, the "financial damage" will spread beyond stockholders to "burn banks, investment funds, and even insurance companies that made loans," he continued.

"The contagion across financial markets will remind us of the GFC," he added.

The dot-com crash wiped out thousands of startups, and even future world-beaters such as Amazon saw stock-price declines of over 90%.

The collapse of the mid-2000s housing bubble and the ensuing financial crisis saw Lehman Brothers go bankrupt, AIG and Bear Stearns bailed out, and the global economy plunge into recession.

Gordon has been a vocal skeptic of the AI boom for years. He told Business Insider in April that the market had "fabricated its own universe" where AI buzz trumps threats like war or inflation.

He said last summer that the huge amount of money riding on the AI theme meant more investors will suffer than in the dot-com crash, and "their suffering will be more painful."

title: Feared in attack, light at the back - why Liverpool's transfer window leaves questions
description: Feared in attack but light at the back? Liverpool have spent more than £200m in the transfer window but questions remain over whether the squad has enough depth.
fullText:
All summer, Andoni Iraola has said that he will be "comfortable" come the start of September when the transfer window is over and he has certainty over his squad.

Senior figures at Liverpool said from the outset that this was never going to be a transfer window like last summer, when the club spent a then record £415m under Arne Slot and broke the British transfer record twice by signing Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak.

Last summer, Liverpool also made £188m from selling players such as Luis Diaz, Darwin Nunez and Jarell Quansah and ended the window with a net spend of £227m.

If you include Jeremy Jacquet (a deal confirmed in January), then Liverpool's net spend is not hugely dissimilar this summer at just under £200m - having also signed Victor Munoz, Ronald Araujo on loan and Bradley Barcola for a combined total of £217.5m.

But they have lost senior figures with Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate all leaving for free and Curtis Jones moving to Inter Milan in a deal worth £30m. Liverpool then rejected a bid worth £80m from Manchester City for Cody Gakpo as they were unable to get a replacement.

On the basis of their first two Premier League games, there is certainly a feeling that Liverpool have left themselves short after their struggles last season.

Where concern lies is the lack of quality squad depth at the back and the absence of an out-and-out defensive midfielder but Iraola's side will end the window having made the second most expensive signing of the summer in France forward Barcola, who chose the Reds despite interest from other clubs including Arsenal.

Sources at Paris St-Germain described the Barcola deal - worth £123m - as part of the "greatest super sub window ever" after they made more than £280m in the sales of five players - including Goncalo Ramos, Lee Kang-in, Randal Kolo Muani and Ibrahim Mbaye - who often featured on the bench last season.

Despite struggling for the game time he wanted at PSG, Liverpool believe they have secured one of the most outstanding wide attacking talents in world football.

Liverpool fans could see their first glimpse of 24-year-old Barcola on Friday when Iraola's side travel to Ipswich. And there is a belief inside the club that the combined £364m trio of Wirtz, Isak and Barcola could become one of the most feared attacks in Europe.

Anfield needs some excitement after a below-par campaign last season which ultimately saw Slot lose the support of the fanbase and his job, a year after winning the Premier League.

Liverpool conceded twice in both league games so far and Iraola will be worried by how easily his side have been cut open.

Defensively, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley are sidelined with long-term injuries and Joe Gomez's pre-season injury prompted Liverpool to bring in Araujo on loan from Barcelona.

The experienced Uruguayan, 27, is a stop-gap for now but Liverpool have an option to buy him for £47m next summer, when Virgil van Dijk's current contract expires.

Meanwhile, Leoni, 19, and Jacquet, 21, are viewed internally as two of the best young centre-backs in Europe. Liverpool are well stocked in that department when you include promising teenage defenders like Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who impressed in pre-season.

The signing of 18-year-old goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans from Genk in a deal that could go up to £30m is also one for the future. Bayern Munich were also interested in the 6ft 7in Belgian and with Alisson’s contract expiring next summer and Giorgi Mamardashvili struggling to make an impact so far, Brughmans could be an option in the 2027-28 season. He is a product of the Genk academy which also developed Thibaut Courtois.

Milos Kerkez has had an underwhelming start to the campaign at left-back but the hope is that he can peak under Iraola, whom he worked with previously at Bournemouth.

On the right, Jeremie Frimpong has struggled to convince so far and Liverpool reportedly failed in an attempt to bring Malo Gusto on loan from Chelsea on deadline day.

Liverpool are willing to wait until Bradley returns from his knee injury but it is an area of worry. Araujo can also play at right-back and so can Dominik Szoboszlai, if needed.

In midfield, Iraola suggested it was not a personnel problem when Newcastle hit Liverpool on the counter twice at St James' Park.

But former Liverpool striker Daniel Sturridge, working on the game as a pundit, said that his old team has needed a defensive midfielder for three years.

Liverpool have not had a genuine number six since Fabinho left in 2023 but senior figures at the club are content with the midfield options for now.

Both Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch signed new long-term deals this year while Alexis Mac Allister, who Manchester City were interested in, is staying. Iraola will also have Wataru Endo and 19-year-old Trey Nyoni available.

The understanding is that any permanent move for a midfielder would only happen in January or next summer. Liverpool did look at Lamine Camara but there was no plan to buy a midfielder this summer.

The average age of Liverpool's first-team signings across the past two windows is 22 and that suggests a long-term approach at Anfield. But, given their struggles in their first two games, this feels like a squad that could have done with more additions this summer.

The club's Champions League campaign begins on 10 September, meaning two games per week most of the time and that will be a new challenge for Iraola.

Liverpool believe they will be better placed once players are back from injury but only time will tell if this squad is strong enough to compete on all four fronts.

title: Five moments that shaped Taylor's legendary career
description: From writing a letter to her idol as a 10-year-old to messaging a promoter on social media, here are five sliding doors moments that helped shape Katie Taylor’s career.
fullText:
On Saturday, Katie Taylor steps through the ropes at an 82,000-capacity Croke Park to face France's Flora Pili in her farewell fight.

Victory on the hallowed Dublin turf would write one final fairytale chapter - a chance to bow out as undisputed light-welterweight champion and put the seal on a career that has revolutionised women's sport.

There have been countless moments that have shaped the 40-year-old's journey.

From a childhood letter to a Twitter direct message, these are five sliding doors moments in the making of an Irish icon.

Long before Taylor became Olympic champion, she was a 10-year-old girl in Bray who simply wanted to box.

There was nowhere for her to go though. Women's boxing was unsanctioned in Ireland, absent from the Olympic programme and devoid of any clear professional pathway.

But there was Deirdre Gogarty. Having relocated to the United States, she became Ireland's first female professional world champion in 1997 when she defeated Bonnie Canino for the WIBF featherweight title in Louisiana.

"How did you do it when everyone tried to stop you?" a 10-year-old Taylor asked in a letter sent to her hero.

"If you keep working at it and keep showing your skills, somebody's going to say 'we've got to let this girl box'," Gogarty replied.

Reflecting on the letter years later, Gogarty added: "It's mind-blowing. Especially when she wrote, 'maybe one day they'll let us box in the Olympics'."

Had that letter never been written, Taylor might still have found her way to the top, but Gogarty offered hope when none seemingly existed.

When the International Olympic Committee was undecided on including women's boxing at the Games, Taylor was brought in for showcase events in front of sceptical officials in Chicago. Her dazzling displays dismantled every argument.

"Katie won't say this, and I've been holding back from saying this, but single-handedly, Katie Taylor got women's boxing into the Olympics," her manager Brian Peters says.

Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at the London 2012 Games and Taylor claimed lightweight gold.

Four years later in Rio, however, that amateur journey ended when a split-decision quarter-final defeat shattered Taylor's title defence. She was at a crossroads - rebuild for another Olympic cycle or turn professional in an era where women's pro boxing was still neglected.

"It was probably the worst year of my career," Taylor later admitted. "I needed a change. I needed a new mindset."

Had she secured a second Olympic gold, the motivation to dive into the pro ranks might have evaporated. Instead, the sting of defeat forced reinvention.

Turning professional was one thing, but securing both the right team and commercial backing was another challenge.

First came manager Peters, who initially stepped in out of concern for her future.

"I only took her on not to see her end up with people who didn't know what they were doing," Peters says.

On 4 October 2016, Taylor sent Matchroom's Eddie Hearn a direct message on Twitter, now known as X, asking if he would consider promoting her. Hearn replied 24 hours later, inviting Taylor, Peters, and her mother Bridget to a London restaurant. Hearn even borrowed his father's car to impress Taylor.

The charm offensive worked and Taylor made her debut at Wembley Arena a month later.

In a sport notorious for fractured relationships and bitter splits, Taylor's core team has remained the same from day one with Peters, Hearn and trainer Ross Enamait.

"In a business full of egos, she's stayed loyal to everyone around her and remained the most humble person you could ever meet," Peters says.

Had Hearn dismissed that DM - or had Taylor lacked the enduring loyalty that kept the same tight-knit team in her corner for a decade - the promotional engine that transformed women's boxing might never have started.

Returning to MSG to face seven-division title winner Amanda Serrano presented a different magnitude of threat.

Their blockbuster marked the first time two women headlined the storied New York venue. In front of a sellout crowd of 19,187, Taylor claimed a split-decision victory in what was widely hailed as the fight of the year.

Had one scorecard leaned the other way or had the bout failed to deliver on its enormous hype, the momentum behind women's mega-fights would have stalled.

Instead, the victory spawned a record-breaking rivalry. Their 2024 rematch drew global viewing figures on Netflix on the undercard of Jake Paul v Mike Tyson, before Taylor sealed the trilogy at the Garden in 2025.

Coverage on Radio 5 Sports Extra from 19:00 BST, then 5 Live from 22:00. Ringwalks for main event expected between 22:00 and 22:30.

Taylor's first professional defeat came in May 2023 at Dublin's 3Arena when she was outpointed by Chantelle Cameron for the undisputed light-welterweight belts.

At 36, questions around retirement surfaced.

In the ring immediately following the defeat, Peters says he told his fighter to congratulate Cameron and ask for the rematch.

Six months later, Taylor delivered a masterclass in grit, claiming a majority decision to become a two-weight undisputed champion.

"The pressure was immense," Peters says.

"For all she had done, her legacy was suddenly questioned. Had Chantelle won the rematch, who knows what would have happened?"

Croke Park is not really a sixth sliding door but rather the final pay-off.

After beating Serrano in last year's trilogy decider, Taylor quietly decided she was done.

"She actually retired that night," Peters says. "She said, 'We convincingly beat Serrano - where do we go from there?' I said I'll agree on one condition."

That condition was Croke Park or nothing.

"Croke Park - no disrespect to Wembley - is the greatest stadium in the world," Peters says. "You cut an Irish person and they'll bleed Croke Park."

Peters insists there will be no change of heart - no Cameron trilogy and no comebacks.

"When Katie gives her word, that is it," he says.

Regardless of Saturday's result, Taylor will be remembered as a pioneer who kicked open the door for women's boxing.

title: UN pushes nations to consider slavery reparations but legal group says idea 'not going to fly in the US'
description: The United Nations says countries are legally obliged to consider slavery reparations and implement restorative justice for racial discrimination.
fullText:
The United Nations said on Monday that countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and other measures to address what it says is the enduring legacy of racial discrimination, but an attorney seeking to shut down the effort insists it won't work in the U.S.

The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) is calling on "states to implement comprehensive restorative justice, combining compensation, restitution, rehabilitation and structural reforms," the UN News reported.

"Irrespective of the legal characterization of the original historical acts, States Parties remain bound by their present obligations under the Convention to address structural inequalities," the U.N. document states.

Guidance published by CERD stated that the obligations stem from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed during the slave trade era.

"It's just outrageous that the United Nations comes in and tells countries that they have to give free money away to their citizens," Michael Bekesha, a senior attorney at Judicial Watch, told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, who are they to say what we can and can't do? The bigger issue for Judicial Watch and something we'll be watching is if the States were ever to do something like this, they would have to follow our Constitution and our laws, and the U.N. doesn't care about that… whatever the U.N. is thinking isn't going to be constitutional and is not going to fly in the United States."

Bekesha made the comments after the DOJ joined their class action lawsuit challenging the Local Reparations Restorative Housing Program in the City of Evanston, Illinois.

Trump Admin Vows To Stop Reparations Programs, Accuses Officials Of 'Virtue Signaling' To Get 'Votes'

The DOJ contends the Chicago suburb's initiative unlawfully distributes public benefits based strictly on race and ancestry. The DOJ's proposed complaint alleges that the program violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment, as well as the Fair Housing Act, because the housing-related financial assistance is distributed on the basis of race.

The litigation began in May 2024 when Judicial Watch, a conservative legal group, filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of six non-Black descendants of Evanston residents, arguing they were unconstitutionally excluded from the program.

The announcement came after the U.N. General Assembly adopted a resolution earlier this year declaring the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity and for member states to pursue reparations to rectify "historical wrongs."

The implementation of reparations has been a growing trend in the United States, spanning from the East to West Coast.

Evanston, Illinois was the first U.S. municipality to establish a reparations program and later began providing $25,000 benefits to eligible Black residents and descendants to address the city's history of housing discrimination.

Despite efforts to issue reparations, some of these programs are facing obstacles due to budgetary or legal pressures. While some states and local governments push for reparations, "financial compensation alone is not sufficient," according to the CERD.

The committee additionally called for comprehensive measures beyond financial compensation.

"It also advocates for comprehensive and far-reaching remedial measures, both financial, non-financial and structural, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-recurrence," UN News reported.

Reparations can take many forms but broadly refer to payments or other compensation intended to address harms suffered by Black Americans and their descendants because of slavery or discriminatory government policies.

"To ensure the effectiveness of reparations, they advocate the implementation of national action plans with specific deadlines, developed in consultation with people of African descent and the committees in charge of reparations," UN News reported.

Bekesha added that reparations are by nature discriminatory.

"If the Evanston case of Judicial Watch and the United States were to win this case, it would show not only the United Nations but every other state and city in the United States that you cannot in the United States provide benefits to individuals solely based on the color of their skin," Bekesha said.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he is nominating acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao for the permanent job, giving the Navy combat veteran the nod as concerns have emerged that some sailors have been stretched to the limit during the Iran war.

Cao has been serving as acting Navy secretary since John Phelan departed the job unexpectedly and without explanation in late April. Unlike Phelan, who had not served in the military or had a civilian leadership role in the service, Cao spent 25 years in the Navy as a special operations officer and went on to serve with SEAL teams and special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan.

"I am pleased to nominate a true WARRIOR," Trump wrote on social media, prodding the Senate "to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP."

Cao on social media called it the "honor of a lifetime to lead the great warriors of the Navy and Marine Corps team."

Cao's nomination comes as some, including Democrats in Congress, believe Trump has been overtaxing the Navy. The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier's nine-month deployment to support the Iran war has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.

Concerns grew about the Lincoln's deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products. Several Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the ship.

Cao served as Navy undersecretary before his current role. He championed returning to duty service members who refused a Biden-era mandate to take the COVID-19 vaccine. The Trump loyalist also said he had no problem with the Navy's demonstration squadron, the Blue Angels, flying so low over a crowded Florida beach in July that chairs and tents went flying.

Cao's nomination also comes at a time of upheaval in the top ranks of the U.S. military. In the latest example, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitted his resignation this week amid widespread reports of tension between him and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

(NewsNation) — A routine highway rest stop check turned into a rescue for an Ohio State Highway Patrol trooper.

Trooper John Kronander of the Medina Post was on patrol Aug. 23 in Guilford Township when he found a puppy abandoned in a crate at a rest stop off I-76 eastbound.

"He noticed a little cage off on the right-hand side that was kind of away from all the traffic," Sgt. Jeremy Kindler told NewsNation local affiliate Fox 8 Cleveland. "There was no trucks around. When he noticed that, he saw like a cardboard box on top, and he saw some movement in it."

When Kronander went over and lifted the cardboard box, he found the puppy locked in a crate with no food or water.

"We'll get you out of here, okay?" said the trooper to the puppy on body camera footage released from the rescue. "Someone left you? It's okay. How long have you been here?"

To his surprise, the puppy wasn't afraid and immediately began to play with him.

"Oh, you pawing me? Oh, oh my gosh. Are you pawing me?" Kronander said to the puppy. "Want to go with me?"

Kronander took the puppy back to the patrol post, where they gave him food and water and contacted the local animal shelter.

The puppy was taken in by the Medina County SPCA, which named him Miles. The shelter believes he is about 3 to 4 months old. The shelter told Fox 8 that Miles will be neutered this week and should be available for adoption next week.

In the meantime, the Ohio State Highway Patrol is reviewing surveillance footage from the area to identify who abandoned him.

title: India’s power demand is surging, but some solar energy is going to waste
description: When India’s power demand surged at the height of summer, the country struggled to meet evening needs as air conditioners ran longer amid hotter nights.  Despite this demand, some renewable energy pro...
fullText:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — When India's power demand surged at the height of summer, the country struggled to meet evening needs as air conditioners ran longer amid hotter nights. Despite this demand, some renewable energy providers were told to limit their output because the country had more clean electricity available than its grid could safely handle.

In the last 15 months, India curtailed nearly 11 terawatt-hours of solar generation — enough electricity to power about 10 million homes, according to government data and research by energy think tank Ember. That solar power went unused even as extreme heat and poor monsoon rains drove up demand for power in India for cooling and pumping groundwater for agriculture.

India, the world's most populous country and one of the largest emitters of climate-polluting gases, is rapidly adding clean energy, especially solar, to its power mix. However, it can't use all the clean power it could generate because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity and the technical difficulty of shifting between fossil power and renewables.

Energy experts say that contradiction points to the next big challenge for India's energy transition. Building solar and wind farms is no longer enough. India also needs more transmission lines to move electricity across the country, batteries to store renewable power until it is needed and a more flexible power system that can quickly adjust as wind and solar output rises or falls.

"We're in a stage where some of the biggest hurdles in renewables are starting to hit us," said Neshwin Rodrigues, an energy analyst at Ember.

India has more than 300 gigawatts of clean power capacity, more than half its total installed electricity capacity. But coal still produces most of the country's electricity.

Experts said the main reason for this is curtailment — when a wind or solar plant could produce electricity but is ordered to reduce or stop generation as the grid cannot take the power.

Rodrigues said that when solar generation surges in the afternoon, it's difficult for coal units to reduce their output because they are relatively inflexible and cannot ramp down quickly without compromising efficiency, increasing costs or risking operational problems.

Trying to make thermal power plants flexible and adapt to increasing supply from clean energy sources "is like asking an elephant to dance," said Vinay Pabba, CEO of Hyderabad-based renewable energy company Vibrant Energy.

Pabba said curtailment results in losses for clean power developers. "We get paid only for what we put on the grid," he said.

The high concentration of renewable generation in western India has also meant that transmission lines in that part of the country get congested quickly. The western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan account for nearly 50% of India's solar power capacity.

"When solar peaks, usually in the afternoon, there is a limited pipe to evacuate it," said Pabba.

Another risk of not building storage quickly is that dirty fuels get used more. "Without enough storage, India risks keeping coal plants running even when cheap renewable power is available," said Vibhuti Garg, South Asia director at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

While a solar or wind farm can sometimes be completed within two years, building new power lines can take a minimum of three years, according to energy experts.

India has achieved only about 80% of its annual transmission construction targets over the past five years, research by Ember has found.

Spreading more renewable development across other parts of the country, while adding more wind and smaller local solar projects, could reduce pressure on crowded transmission corridors and make the electricity supply more balanced throughout the day, said Disha Agarwal, an energy analyst at the New Delhi-based Council on Energy, Environment and Water.

Agarwal said the challenge is likely to become more difficult as renewable capacity keeps rising.

India is aiming for 500 gigawatts of clean electricity capacity by 2030. Also, Indian policymakers expect nearly 70% of India's installed power capacity to come from nonfossil sources by 2036.

A study released earlier this month by the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, found that renewable power backed by batteries can provide electricity with reliability approaching that of conventional power plants at a price researchers said is lower than the price of power from new coal-fired plants.

Batteries make it possible to store solar electricity when it is abundant in the afternoon and discharge it after sunset, when demand remains high.

But India's storage sector remains far smaller than what planners said will eventually be required.

"If we try to increase the solar installations without solving for energy storage, it is only going to lead to curtailment," said Ankit Mittal, CEO of battery storage company Ingro Energy.

Mittal said India is trying to transform several parts of its electricity system simultaneously as power demand rises. "Things that were supposed to happen over decades" are now happening at once, he said.

The government said in July that it had about 3 gigawatts of battery storage and 7.4 gigawatts of operational pumped-storage capacity. It expects India's storage needs to reach about 74 gigawatts by 2032.

"If high quality energy storage projects are not built, we could be adding an additional layer of risk to grid operations while also decelerating our nation's ability to achieve our energy transition targets," said Avinash Rao, CEO of Mahindra Susten, a leading renewable energy company in India.

Rodrigues, the energy analyst, said batteries can be built much more quickly than major transmission infrastructure, making them one of the fastest options for easing some immediate constraints.

Industry stakeholders said that few, if any, foresaw the incredible increase in demand happening as the country's transportation and other major sectors electrify and data centers are built.

"None of us saw it coming. If we had seen it coming, we would have probably planned our way around it," said Pabba of Vibrant Energy.
